title: The System Design Interview
objectives: A 45-minute collaborative conversation where you clarify, estimate, sketch, and defend trade-offs.

cards.title: What interviewers grade
cards.body: Interviewers grade how you think, not a single right diagram. They watch for: clarifying scope, sensible numbers, a clear API, a clean high-level design, a deep dive into one hard part, and honest trade-offs.

cards.title: Six stages on a 45-minute clock
cards.body: Every interview in this course uses the same six stages. API design is its own stage: agreeing the two or three key endpoints before drawing boxes fixes what the design has to serve. Interview mode and the Interview Playbook run this exact plan.

cards.title: Misconception: there is one right answer
cards.body: Many candidates try to reach the 'correct' architecture. There isn't one. Two strong candidates can draw different designs for the same prompt and both pass, because the interviewer grades whether each choice follows from the stated requirements and numbers, and whether you can say what it costs.

cards.title: Trap: designing before scoping
cards.body: Jumping straight into Kafka and microservices before asking what the product does. Spend roughly the first five minutes on requirements; the interviewer may steer you sooner.

cards.title: Worked example: the first five minutes
cards.body: Interviewer: “Design a URL shortener.” Good clarifying questions: Who creates links, and roughly how many per day? Do links expire? Custom aliases? Is click analytics in scope? A strong opening answer: “I’ll assume 100M new links a month, about 100 reads per write, redirects under 50 ms, links never expire, analytics out of scope. Let me size that before drawing anything.”

questions.prompt: The interviewer says “Design a URL shortener.” What is the strongest first move?

choices.label: Propose Kafka and microservices up front so the design can scale later
Ask who creates links, roughly how many per day, and whether links expire
Estimate storage straight away using a guessed user count
Sketch the links table schema so there is something concrete to discuss

questions.explanation: Scope first. The number of links, the read/write ratio and expiry change every later choice.

questions.prompt: Order the six stages of a 45-minute design interview.
questions.explanation: Requirements drive the numbers, the numbers and the API define what the design must serve, and the deep dive tests it. Wrap-up closes with trade-offs.

questions.prompt: What is the interviewer mainly grading?

choices.label: How many technologies you can name in 45 minutes
Whether your diagram matches the company’s real architecture
How you scope the problem, reason with numbers and defend trade-offs
Whether every component is designed in full detail

questions.explanation: There is no single right diagram. Interviewers watch the reasoning.

questions.prompt: For a URL shortener, which clarifying question changes the design most?

choices.label: Should short codes use uppercase letters?
Which cloud provider does the team prefer?
Which programming language should the redirect service use?
How many new links a day, and roughly how many reads per write?

questions.explanation: Volume and read/write ratio decide caching, storage and ID generation. The others are details you can decide later.

questions.prompt: How should you spend the first five minutes of “Design WhatsApp”?

approaches.label: Ask every question you can think of
approaches.description: Cover each edge case before drawing

approaches.label: Ask 3–4 scoping questions, then state assumptions
approaches.description: Users, core features, scale, out of scope

rationaleOptions.label: Scale and features drive every later choice
Interviewers expect every edge case settled before any design
Stating assumptions lets the interviewer correct you early

rationaleConflicts.r3: Time is limited. Ask what changes the design, then move on; edge cases come up in the deep dive.

questions.explanation: Short, targeted questions plus stated assumptions keep the rest of the interview grounded.

flashcards.front: What is graded in a design round?
flashcards.back: Structured thinking, trade-offs, communication — not a single perfect diagram.
Clarify functional + non-functional requirements and scope.

flashcards.front: The six interview stages and their minutes?
flashcards.back: Requirements 0–5, estimation 5–10, API 10–15, high-level design 15–25, deep dive 25–40, wrap-up 40–45.

title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
objectives: Turn users into QPS, storage and bandwidth with rounded math: 1 day ≈ 10^5 seconds.

cards.title: The estimation formulas
cards.body: QPS = DAU × actions per user ÷ 86,400. Peak = average × a peak factor you assume and say out loud (for example 2–3× for a daily curve, 10×+ for event spikes). Storage = writes/day × object size × retention. Round aggressively; the order of magnitude matters.

cards.title: From users to peak QPS
cards.body: Multiply users by actions, divide by the seconds in a day, then multiply by the peak factor you assume for this product.

cards.title: Worked example: QPS, storage and bandwidth for a chat app
cards.body: Assume: 50 million DAU; 40 messages sent per user per day; 100 bytes per message body, 200 bytes with metadata; Messages kept for 1 year, stored 3× for replication; Peak factor 3× (an example assumption for a daily curve; event spikes could be higher).
steps: Average write QPS = 2B ÷ 86,400 ≈ 23,000 per second (with the 10⁵ shortcut: 20,000).
Peak write QPS ≈ 23,000 × 3 ≈ 70,000 per second, under the assumed 3× peak.
Storage per day = 2 billion messages × 200 bytes = 400 GB. Per year: 400 GB × 365 ≈ 146 TB, and with 3 replicas ≈ 440 TB.
Ingress at peak = 70,000 messages/s × 200 bytes = 14 MB/s ≈ 112 Mbit/s.
cards.note: About 23K average and 70K peak writes per second, and roughly 150 TB a year of raw messages (about 440 TB with replication). Raw message ingress is relatively modest under these assumptions; real network traffic is several times higher once fan-out to each recipient, replication, protocol overhead and media are added. Whether 70K writes/s fits on one database depends on the hardware (CPU, NVMe), the cost of each write (row size, number of indexes), durability settings (fsync per commit or group commit), batching, and the engine (B-tree or LSM). Distribute when measurements show one node lacks headroom at peak, when one machine cannot hold the data (hundreds of TB here does force splitting storage), or when you need to survive a node failure without losing write capacity.

cards.title: Trap: forgetting the peak
cards.body: Designing for the average. Traffic in India is spiky around cricket finals, Big Billion Days and Tatkal at 10 AM, so state a peak factor for the workload and ask whether events push it higher.

questions.prompt: 10M daily users each make 10 requests a day. Roughly what is the average QPS?
A chat app has 50M daily users sending 40 messages a day each. Estimate average messages per second (in thousands).
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 23K/s is roughly ten times what one well-tuned app server handles for simple writes, so even the average needs a small fleet, and the peak you assume sets the real size.

questions.prompt: A photo app stores 2M new photos a day at 500 KB each. How much storage is added per year, in TB?
questions.workedAnswer: 2M × 500 KB = 1 TB a day; 1 TB × 365 = 365 TB a year.
questions.explanation: Design implication: 365 TB a year, before replicas and thumbnails, rules out keeping photos on app servers or in the database. Store the bytes in object storage and keep only metadata in the database.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site averages 2,000 QPS, but sales open at 10 AM. What should you design for?

choices.label: A stated peak several times the average, for example 10–20K QPS
2,000 × 86,400, the daily total
2,000 QPS, since the average already includes the 10 AM spike
Exactly 2× the average, the standard peak factor for every system

questions.explanation: Averages hide spikes. A peak factor is a workload assumption you state and confirm: about 2–3× for a smooth daily curve, 10× or more when sales open.

questions.prompt: Order the steps from daily users to the number you design for.
questions.explanation: Users × actions gives daily volume; divide by seconds per day; then multiply for peak.

flashcards.front: How do you pick a peak factor?
flashcards.back: It is an assumption you state, not a constant: for example 2–3× for a daily curve, 10× or more for events. Ask the interviewer.

title: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal + Load Balancers
objectives: Scale up with a bigger box or scale out with more boxes behind a load balancer.

cards.title: Scale up or scale out
cards.body: Vertical scaling is simple but hits a ceiling and is a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling needs stateless services, a load balancer and partitioned data. It adds capacity, and it only adds availability if the copies fail independently and traffic is routed away from dead ones (health checks, no shared single database). Gains are rarely linear: shared state, coordination and hot keys eat into them.

cards.title: Growing from one server to many
cards.body: Scale up first because it is simple; before scaling out, move state off the servers so any instance can serve any request.

cards.title: Worked example: how many app servers for a peak?
cards.body: Assume: Peak 60,000 requests per second; One app server handles about 2,000 requests per second at a safe 60–70% CPU (measure this in a load test); Each server is 99.9% available on its own.
steps: Add headroom to survive losing one availability zone of three: 30 ÷ (2/3) = 45 servers.
Availability of one server = 99.9%: about 8.8 hours of downtime a year (0.001 × 8,760 h).

With two independent servers behind a load balancer, both are down at once with probability 0.001² = 10^-6, so the app tier is about 99.9999% available, ignoring the load balancer and correlated failures.
cards.note: About 30 servers for raw load and about 45 to stay up through a zone failure. Redundancy, not size, is what moves availability from 'three nines' towards 'six nines'; correlated failures and shared dependencies stop you getting the full benefit.

cards.title: Trap: in-memory sessions
cards.body: Saying "just add servers" while keeping session state in server memory. Stateless first, then scale out.

questions.prompt: What must be true before app servers can scale horizontally easily?

choices.label: Sticky sessions pin every user to one server for good
Session state lives outside the app servers (Redis or signed tokens)
Each server keeps its own full copy of the database
All servers run on identical hardware and OS versions

questions.explanation: If any server can handle any request, the balancer can spread load and servers can come and go.

questions.prompt: What is the main limit of vertical scaling?

choices.label: It adds CPU cores, but memory and disk cannot grow
Load balancers cannot route traffic to a bigger server
A hardware ceiling, and the one machine is still a single point of failure
It forces you to rewrite the app to be fully stateless

questions.explanation: A bigger box is simple but finite, and it is still one box.

questions.prompt: Four app servers sit behind a load balancer, all using one primary database. Has availability improved?

choices.label: No: adding app servers never changes availability, only speed
Yes: four app servers make the whole system four times as available
Yes, fully, as long as the balancer uses round robin across all four
Partly: an app server can fail safely, but the single database is still a single point of failure

questions.explanation: Copies only raise availability where failures are independent and traffic is routed away from the dead one.

questions.prompt: Order the usual path from one server to many.
questions.explanation: Scale up while it is cheap; move state out before scaling out.

questions.prompt: A shop runs on one large server at 80% CPU. A sale in three weeks is expected to bring 5× traffic.
constraints: The next instance size is only 2× bigger
Sessions live in server memory today

approaches.label: Move sessions to Redis, then run several servers behind a load balancer

rationaleOptions.label: The biggest box gives 2×, short of the 5× needed
Moving sessions out first lets any server take any request
Adding app servers also makes the database faster

rationaleConflicts.r3: The database is shared; more app servers add load to it rather than speeding it up.

questions.explanation: The bottleneck is app CPU, so scale the app tier out once it is stateless.

flashcards.back: Hardware ceiling and single point of failure.
Stateless services (externalise sessions).

title: OSI & TCP/IP
objectives: Place HTTP, TLS, TCP/UDP and IP in the right layer
Explain what a TCP handshake costs a request
Choose TCP or UDP for a given workload

cards.title: Why layers matter
cards.body: Interviewers rarely ask for all seven OSI layers. They ask which layer a component works at: an L4 load balancer sees IPs and ports, an L7 one sees HTTP paths and headers. Knowing the layer tells you what a box can and cannot do.

cards.title: The four layers you actually use
cards.body: Application (HTTP, gRPC, DNS) → Transport (TCP, UDP) → Internet (IP) → Link (Ethernet, Wi-Fi). TCP gives ordered, reliable byte streams with retransmits; UDP gives fire-and-forget datagrams with no ordering.

cards.title: A new HTTPS connection
cards.body: Before the first byte, a cold HTTPS request pays for a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake, each costing round trips.

cards.title: Trap: ignoring round trips
cards.body: Ignoring round trips. From Mumbai to a us-east server one RTT is roughly 200 ms, so a cold HTTPS connection spends about 400 ms before the first byte. Keep-alive, connection pooling and edge termination exist to avoid paying that on every request.

questions.prompt: A multiplayer game sends each player’s position 20 times a second; a lost update does not matter because the next one replaces it. Which transport fits best?

choices.label: UDP (or a UDP-based protocol such as QUIC)
TCP, so every stale update is retransmitted in order
A new TCP connection for each update

questions.explanation: Retransmitting stale data only adds delay. TCP works, but it is not the best fit. (A browser score widget is different: it usually uses SSE or WebSockets over HTTP, as lesson 10 shows.)

questions.prompt: An L4 load balancer can route on which of these?

choices.label: The Authorization header
The URL path, such as /api
Destination IP and port
A cookie set by the app

questions.explanation: L4 sees transport information only. Paths, headers and cookies are HTTP, which is L7.

questions.prompt: Where does TLS sit in a typical HTTPS request?

choices.label: Below IP, so routers cannot see addresses
Above HTTP, inside the JSON body
Between TCP and HTTP: it encrypts the byte stream TCP carries
Inside DNS, during name resolution

questions.explanation: TLS runs on TCP and under HTTP. QUIC (HTTP/3) folds transport and TLS together over UDP.

questions.prompt: Order what happens before a brand-new HTTPS request can be sent.
questions.explanation: Resolve the name, open the connection, encrypt it, then send.

questions.prompt: Mumbai to us-east is about 200 ms round trip. With DNS cached, how many ms do the TCP and TLS 1.3 handshakes take before the request can be sent?
questions.workedAnswer: TCP 1 RTT + TLS 1.3 1 RTT = 2 × 200 ms = 400 ms.
questions.explanation: Design implication: 400 ms of handshakes before the first byte is why you terminate TLS close to users (a CDN or edge PoP) and reuse connections instead of opening a new one per request.

flashcards.front: Which transport gives ordered, reliable delivery?
flashcards.back: TCP. UDP gives unordered datagrams with no retransmits.

flashcards.front: What does an L4 load balancer see?
flashcards.back: IP addresses and ports, not HTTP paths or headers.
Each new HTTPS connection pays TCP + TLS round trips before the first byte.

title: TCP vs UDP
objectives: Explain what TCP guarantees and what UDP leaves to the app
Recognise head-of-line blocking
Choose a transport for a real workload

cards.title: What each gives you
cards.body: TCP is a connection: a three-way handshake, then an ordered, reliable byte stream with retransmits and congestion control. UDP sends independent datagrams: no handshake, no ordering, no retransmits. The app decides what to do about loss.

cards.title: Head-of-line blocking
cards.body: TCP delivers bytes in order, so one lost packet stalls everything behind it until it is resent. For live video or game state a late packet is worthless, and UDP lets the app skip it. HTTP/3 runs QUIC over UDP so a loss only stalls its own stream.

cards.title: Opening a TCP connection
cards.body: TCP's three-way handshake opens the connection; sequence numbers then let the receiver spot gaps and the sender retransmit lost segments.

cards.title: Choosing
cards.body: TCP for anything that must arrive complete: APIs, payments, file transfer, chat history. UDP (often through QUIC or WebRTC) for real-time voice, video and game state, and for small DNS queries, where speed beats completeness.

cards.title: Trap: 'UDP is faster'
cards.body: Saying UDP is “faster” and stopping there. It skips handshakes and waiting on retransmits, but if you need reliability you must rebuild it in the app, which is exactly what QUIC does.

questions.prompt: Which workload fits UDP better than TCP?

choices.label: Submitting a UPI payment
Loading chat history when the app opens
Uploading a 2 GB file to object storage
Voice on a video call, where a late packet is useless

questions.explanation: Real-time media prefers dropping late packets over waiting for them.

questions.prompt: Why does one lost packet hurt a TCP stream carrying many requests?

choices.label: The client must redo the three-way handshake
Everything behind it waits until it is retransmitted (head-of-line blocking)
TCP closes the connection whenever a packet is lost
The receiver discards all later packets permanently

questions.explanation: In-order delivery means later bytes cannot be handed to the app until the gap is filled.

questions.prompt: Order the start of a TCP connection.
questions.explanation: The handshake costs one round trip before any data.

questions.prompt: Why does HTTP/3 run on QUIC over UDP?

choices.label: So it can skip encryption and save a round trip
Because TCP cannot carry compressed HTTP headers
So a loss on one stream does not stall the others, with TLS built in
Because UDP itself guarantees delivery and ordering

questions.explanation: QUIC adds reliability per stream on top of UDP, avoiding TCP-level head-of-line blocking.

questions.prompt: Pick transports for a multiplayer racing game.
constraints: Position updates 20 times a second per player
The game also has chat and in-app purchases

approaches.label: UDP for positions, TCP (HTTPS) for chat and purchases
approaches.description: Match each message type to its needs

rationaleOptions.label: UDP keeps position updates in order
Purchases must arrive complete and in order
Stale position updates are not worth retransmitting

rationaleConflicts.r3: UDP has no ordering; the game must number updates and drop old ones itself.

questions.explanation: Use each transport where its guarantees match the data.

flashcards.front: Which workload fits UDP better than TCP?
flashcards.back: Voice on a video call, where a late packet is useless. Real-time media prefers dropping late packets over waiting for them.

flashcards.front: Why does one lost packet hurt a TCP stream carrying many requests?
flashcards.back: Everything behind it waits until it is retransmitted (head-of-line blocking). In-order delivery means later bytes cannot be handed to the app until the gap is filled.

flashcards.front: Why does HTTP/3 run on QUIC over UDP?
flashcards.back: So a loss on one stream does not stall the others, with TLS built in. QUIC adds reliability per stream on top of UDP, avoiding TCP-level head-of-line blocking.

title: DNS
objectives: DNS maps names to IPs through a cached hierarchy: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative.

cards.title: How a name becomes an IP
cards.body: Browsers ask a recursive resolver, which walks root → .in/.com TLD → authoritative server and caches by TTL. Low TTLs allow fast failover; high TTLs reduce lookups.

cards.title: One DNS lookup, hop by hop
cards.body: A cache miss walks from the recursive resolver to the root, the TLD and the authoritative server; every answer is cached for its TTL.

cards.title: Worked example: how long does a TTL keep users on a dead region?
cards.body: Assume: A record TTL = 300 s (5 min); The region fails at 10:00:00; Resolver caches filled at random times before the failure.
steps: A resolver that cached the record just before 10:00 keeps serving it until about 10:05.
On average a cached entry has half its TTL left: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 s, so the typical user is stuck for about 2.5 minutes.
Worst case is the full 300 s, plus any client or resolver that ignores the TTL.
With a 24-hour TTL (86,400 s), the average stuck time would be 43,200 s = 12 hours.
cards.note: A 5-minute TTL means roughly 2.5 minutes of average impact and up to 5 minutes (plus stragglers); a 24-hour TTL means up to a day. Choose the TTL from how fast you must move traffic.

cards.title: Trap: long TTLs slow failover
cards.body: Forgetting that DNS caching delays failover. A 24 h TTL means some users hit the dead region for a day.

questions.prompt: Why lower a DNS TTL a day before moving to a new server?

choices.label: So resolvers stop caching the old IP for long and switch quickly
Lower TTLs make each lookup resolve faster
It is required to issue a new TLS certificate
It makes browsers skip the recursive resolver

questions.explanation: Caches keep a record until its TTL expires. A short TTL bounds how long clients use the old address.

questions.prompt: Order a cold DNS lookup.
questions.explanation: The resolver walks the hierarchy and caches each answer.

questions.prompt: On a cold lookup, who walks from the root down to the authoritative server?

choices.label: The root server forwards the query down the chain
The browser contacts each server itself
The authoritative server pushes records to browsers
The recursive resolver (your ISP’s or a public one)

questions.explanation: Browsers ask one resolver; it does the walking and caches the results.

questions.prompt: A record with a 24-hour TTL points at a region that just died. What happens?

choices.label: Browsers automatically try the next region
DNS detects the failure and refreshes every cache within seconds
Some users keep reaching the dead region until their cached record expires, up to a day
The authoritative server pushes the new IP to all resolvers

questions.explanation: DNS is pull-based. Caches keep the old answer until the TTL runs out.

questions.prompt: Pick a TTL for api.example.in.
constraints: Regional failover must take minutes, not hours
Millions of clients, so lookup volume matters

rationaleOptions.label: A few minutes still lets resolvers absorb most lookups
A long TTL is fine because DNS failover is instant
A short TTL bounds how long clients hold a dead IP

rationaleConflicts.r3: Cached records keep sending users to the dead region until the TTL expires.

questions.explanation: Minutes-long TTLs balance failover speed against lookup load.

flashcards.front: What does TTL control in DNS?
flashcards.back: How long resolvers cache the record.
Return different IPs based on user location.

title: HTTP/HTTPS/TLS
objectives: Describe what TLS adds to HTTP
Count the round trips for a new HTTPS connection
Decide where to terminate TLS

cards.title: HTTPS in one sentence
cards.body: HTTPS is HTTP sent over a TLS-encrypted connection. TLS gives confidentiality (nobody can read it), integrity (nobody can change it unnoticed) and server authentication via a certificate chain.

cards.title: The handshake
cards.body: In TLS 1.3 the client and server exchange key shares in one round trip, the client checks the certificate chain, and both sides derive the session keys.

cards.title: Where to terminate TLS
cards.body: Usually at the edge: a CDN or L7 load balancer decrypts, routes on the path, and talks to services over a private network (optionally re-encrypted with mTLS). Terminating close to the user cuts handshake latency.

cards.title: Trap: 'HTTPS makes it secure'
cards.body: Saying HTTPS makes an API secure. It protects data in transit only. You still need authentication, authorization, input validation and rate limiting.

questions.prompt: Your L7 load balancer must route /payments and /catalog to different services. Where should TLS terminate?

choices.label: At the load balancer (or edge), so it can read the HTTP path
Nowhere: plain HTTP is fine inside a data centre, so clients can skip TLS too
At the database, the last hop
Only at each backend, so the balancer never sees plaintext

questions.explanation: An L7 balancer can only route on paths it can read. Re-encrypt to services with mTLS if needed.

questions.prompt: Which statement about HTTPS is accurate?

choices.label: It proves which user is making each request, so no login is needed
It protects data in transit; you still need authentication and authorization
It also encrypts the data at rest inside the database and backups
It blocks SQL injection because the request body is encrypted

questions.explanation: TLS secures the connection, not the application.

questions.prompt: Order the TLS 1.3 handshake.

items.label: Server sends certificate; client verifies chain and CertificateVerify
Finished; switch to application keys for HTTP

questions.explanation: In TLS 1.3 both sides derive handshake keys right after the hellos; the certificate then travels encrypted, the client verifies it, and Finished switches to application keys.

questions.prompt: A user in Chennai reaches an origin in Singapore at 60 ms RTT. On a fresh TLS 1.3 connection, roughly how many ms until the first byte of the response (ignore DNS and server time)?
assumptions: TCP and TLS 1.3 each take one round trip
The request itself takes one more
questions.explanation: Sanity check: three round trips, each one 60 ms. TLS 1.3 resumption (0-RTT) or a nearer edge removes most of that cost on repeat visits.

questions.prompt: What does the server’s certificate chain prove to the browser?

choices.label: That the server is really the owner of the domain you asked for
That the connection will be faster
That the server’s code has no vulnerabilities
That the user is logged in

questions.explanation: Authentication of the server is one of TLS’s three guarantees, with confidentiality and integrity.

flashcards.front: What three things does TLS provide?
flashcards.back: Confidentiality, integrity and server authentication.

flashcards.front: Why terminate TLS at the edge?
flashcards.back: Shorter handshakes for users, and the L7 balancer can route on HTTP paths.
No. It protects data in transit; you still need AuthN and AuthZ.

title: REST API Design
objectives: Resources as nouns, HTTP verbs as actions, proper status codes, pagination and idempotency.

cards.title: Resources, verbs and status codes
cards.body: GET /orders/42, POST /orders, PATCH /orders/42. Use 2xx/4xx/5xx correctly, cursor pagination for large lists, and versioning (/v1). PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not by default.

cards.title: Creating an order over REST
cards.body: A POST is validated, creates the resource, and answers 201 with a Location header pointing at the new order.

cards.title: Worked example: why offset pagination hurts on a large table
cards.body: Assume: Orders table with an index on created_at; Page size 20; User scrolls to page 5,000.
steps: Offset query: OFFSET 99,980 LIMIT 20, because 4,999 pages × 20 = 99,980 rows to skip.
The database walks about 100,000 index entries and discards all but 20.
Cursor query: WHERE created_at < :last_seen ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20 seeks straight to the position and reads about 20 entries.
Work ratio ≈ 100,000 ÷ 20 = 5,000 times more rows touched for the offset version on that page.
cards.note: At deep pages offset pagination does thousands of times more work than a cursor, and it gets worse as users scroll. Use cursors for feeds and long lists.

cards.title: Trap: verbs in URLs, 200 for errors
cards.body: Using verbs in URLs (/getOrder) and returning 200 with an error body. Status codes are part of the contract.

questions.prompt: Which request is idempotent by definition?

choices.label: PUT /orders/42 with the full order
POST /orders
POST /orders/42/items

questions.explanation: Repeating a PUT leaves the same state; POST creates something new each time unless you add idempotency keys.

questions.prompt: Creating an order succeeded. What should the API return?

choices.label: 204 No Content and no way to find the new id
201 Created with a Location header for the new order
302 redirect to the order page
200 OK with {"error": null}

questions.explanation: Status codes are part of the contract; 201 plus Location tells the client where the resource lives.

questions.prompt: Which endpoint follows REST conventions?

choices.label: POST /v1/orders/fetch
GET /v1/orders/42/delete
POST /v1/getOrder?id=42
GET /v1/orders/42

questions.explanation: Resources are nouns; the HTTP method is the verb.

questions.prompt: A user’s order history has 50,000 rows and new orders keep arriving. Which pagination is safest?

choices.label: Return all 50,000 rows and let the client page
Offset-based: ?page=2500&size=20
Cursor-based: ?after=<last seen id>
Return the newest 20 only, with no way to go further

questions.explanation: Cursors stay stable as rows are inserted and do not scan skipped rows.

questions.prompt: Order the handling of a create request.
questions.explanation: Validate before creating; return the new resource’s location.

flashcards.back: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD (and OPTIONS).
Cursor is stable and fast on large, changing lists.

title: gRPC & GraphQL
objectives: GraphQL lets clients pick fields; gRPC gives fast typed RPC over HTTP/2 with protobuf.

cards.title: GraphQL for clients, gRPC between services
cards.body: GraphQL fits varied frontends that need different shapes from one endpoint. gRPC fits service-to-service calls: binary, schema-first, streaming, low latency.

cards.title: One GraphQL query fanning out to gRPC
cards.body: The gateway parses the query, resolvers call services over gRPC, and the response is shaped to exactly the fields asked for.

cards.title: Worked example: the cost of N+1 on a home screen
cards.body: Assume: Home screen shows 50 orders, each with its restaurant; Each database round trip takes 2 ms inside the data centre; Resolvers run one after another.
steps: Naive: 1 query for orders + 50 queries for restaurants = 51 round trips.
Time ≈ 51 × 2 ms = 102 ms of database waiting per request.
Batched with a DataLoader: 1 query for orders + 1 IN query for 50 restaurants = 2 round trips ≈ 4 ms.
At 1,000 requests/s, naive = 51,000 queries/s versus 2,000 queries/s batched.
cards.note: Batching cuts this screen from 51 queries to 2 and the database load by about 25×. Always mention DataLoader-style batching when you propose GraphQL.

cards.title: Trap: unbounded nested queries
cards.body: Using GraphQL without query cost limits — one nested query can fan out into thousands of DB calls (N+1).

questions.prompt: Best fit for low-latency calls between internal services?

choices.label: gRPC with protobuf over HTTP/2
Server-sent events
GraphQL, so each service picks its fields
REST with JSON over a new connection per call

questions.explanation: Binary, schema-first, multiplexed calls suit service-to-service traffic.

questions.prompt: A mobile app and a web dashboard need different fields from the same data. What fits?

choices.label: A separate database for each client
GraphQL, so each client asks for exactly the fields it needs
One REST endpoint returning every field to both
gRPC streaming straight to the browser

questions.explanation: GraphQL lets varied frontends shape their own responses from one endpoint.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL query for 100 posts with their authors makes 101 database calls. What is this, and the fix?

choices.label: A cache stampede: add TTL jitter to the author cache
Normal load for 100 posts: add read replicas
Head-of-line blocking: switch the API to HTTP/3
The N+1 problem: batch the author lookups and cap query cost

questions.explanation: Resolvers that fetch per item multiply calls; batching (a DataLoader) and cost limits contain it.

questions.prompt: Order a request through a GraphQL gateway in front of gRPC services.
questions.explanation: The gateway shapes the response; services stay fast and typed behind it.

questions.prompt: What does “schema-first” mean for gRPC?

choices.label: Clients and servers share a .proto contract and generate code from it
JSON keys are only checked at runtime
The database schema must be designed before the API
Clients send their own schema with each request

questions.explanation: The contract is defined once and both sides are generated from it.

flashcards.back: N+1 queries and expensive nested queries.
Protocol Buffers.

title: Polling/Long Polling/SSE/WebSockets
objectives: Real-time options: polling, long polling, server-sent events (one-way), WebSockets (two-way).

cards.title: Polling, SSE or WebSockets
cards.body: Short polling wastes requests. Long polling holds a request open. SSE streams server→client over HTTP. WebSockets keep a full-duplex connection — needed for chat and live location.

cards.title: Pushing an event to a connected user
cards.body: The gateway holding the user's socket subscribes to their channel, so a published event is routed to that gateway and pushed down the socket.

cards.title: Worked example: polling versus pushing for 1 million live users
cards.body: Assume: 1 million users with the screen open; Short polling every 5 seconds; About 1 real update per user per minute; A tuned WebSocket gateway holds about 100,000 idle connections (often more; measure it).
steps: Useful updates = 1,000,000 ÷ 60 ≈ 16,700 per second, so about 92% of polls return nothing.
With WebSockets, gateways needed for connections = 1,000,000 ÷ 100,000 = 10, plus headroom, say 15.
Messages pushed ≈ 16,700 per second, sent only when something changes.
cards.note: Polling every 5 s costs about 200K requests/s, mostly empty, while pushing costs about 15 gateway servers and about 17K messages/s. At this scale, push wins.

cards.title: Trap: ignoring connection state
cards.body: Ignoring connection state at scale: millions of sockets need dedicated gateway servers and a pub/sub to route messages to the right one.

questions.prompt: A live cricket score only flows from server to client. What fits best?

choices.label: Server-sent events (a one-way stream over HTTP)
Long polling with a 30-second timeout
WebSockets, because every real-time feature needs two-way
Short polling every 100 ms

questions.explanation: SSE is simpler than WebSockets when data only flows one way.

questions.prompt: Which feature most needs WebSockets?

choices.label: A stock price ticker
Order status that changes every few minutes
Chat with typing indicators
A live cricket scoreboard

questions.explanation: Typing indicators and messages flow both ways continuously; the others are server-to-client.

questions.prompt: 1M clients poll every 5 seconds, but data changes about once a minute. What is the main problem?

choices.label: Polling cannot pass through load balancers
The server must hold 1M open connections
Updates arrive out of order
About 200K requests a second, nearly all returning nothing new

questions.explanation: 1M ÷ 5 = 200K requests/s of mostly empty answers. Push or long polling avoids that.

questions.prompt: Order delivery of a chat message over WebSockets at scale.

items.label: Pub/sub routes it to the right gateway
Gateway pushes it to the client

questions.explanation: Gateways hold sockets; pub/sub finds which gateway holds the recipient.

questions.prompt: A chat app keeps all 2M sockets on one gateway server and it hits connection limits. Click the bottleneck.
questions.explanation: Socket state needs a fleet of gateways, with pub/sub routing messages to whichever one holds the user.

flashcards.back: Server to client only.

flashcards.front: How to route a message to a user on a different WS server?
flashcards.back: Pub/sub or a connection registry.

title: LB Algorithms
objectives: Round robin, least connections, weighted, and consistent hashing — pick by workload shape.

cards.title: Matching the algorithm to the traffic
cards.body: Round robin is simple for uniform requests. Least connections suits uneven request lengths. Weighted handles mixed hardware. Hashing (IP or key) gives affinity for caches.

cards.title: Picking a server for each request
cards.body: The balancer applies its algorithm to the healthy pool, forwards the request and updates its counters (connections, weights) for the next pick.

cards.title: Worked example: how many keys move when you add a server?
cards.body: Assume: 10 cache servers, growing to 11; Keys spread uniformly.
steps: Modulo hashing: a key stays put only if hash mod 10 equals hash mod 11, which is true for about 1 key in 11.
So about 10 ÷ 11 ≈ 91% of keys move to a different server, and the cache hit rate collapses.
Consistent hashing: the new server takes over only its share of the ring, about 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 9% of keys.
With 1 billion cached keys, that is about 910 million keys moving versus about 91 million.
cards.note: Adding one server to ten moves about 91% of keys with modulo hashing but only about 9% with consistent hashing. That is why caches and partitions use consistent hashing.

cards.title: Trap: round robin on uneven requests
cards.body: Using round robin when request durations vary wildly; slow servers accumulate a backlog.

questions.prompt: Requests take anywhere from 5 ms to 5 s. Best default algorithm?

choices.label: IP hash
Least connections
Round robin
Random

questions.explanation: With uneven durations, round robin piles slow requests on some servers; least connections adapts.

questions.prompt: A pool has two new 32-core servers and four old 8-core ones. Which algorithm?

choices.label: Weighted, in proportion to capacity
Send everything to the two new servers
IP hash
Plain round robin

questions.explanation: Weights let bigger machines take more traffic without starving the small ones.

questions.prompt: Each server keeps a local cache of user profiles. Which algorithm keeps a user on the same server?

choices.label: Round robin across all servers
Least connections at that moment
Random choice, with retries on miss
Hashing on the user id (consistent hashing)

questions.explanation: Key-based hashing gives affinity, so the local cache stays warm.

questions.prompt: Order how a balancer handles a request.
questions.explanation: Least connections needs those counters updated for the next decision.

questions.prompt: Round robin over three servers; some requests take 5 s. Server B now has a long backlog. Which box should change?
questions.explanation: B is a symptom. Switching the balancer to least connections stops sending it more work while it is busy.

flashcards.back: Requests of uneven duration.
Affinity: same key → same server.

title: L4 vs L7 LB & Health Checks
objectives: L4 routes by IP/port (fast, protocol-agnostic); L7 routes by HTTP content (paths, headers, cookies).

cards.title: What L4 and L7 can see
cards.body: L4 forwards TCP/UDP connections without reading payloads. L7 terminates HTTP, so it can route /api vs /static, do header-based canary routing and TLS termination.

cards.title: Routing a request at L4 and L7
cards.body: L4 decides from IP and port alone; L7 terminates TLS, parses HTTP and matches a path or header rule before forwarding to a pool.

cards.title: Worked example: how many requests fail before a dead server is removed?
cards.body: Assume: 10 backends sharing 1,000 requests per second evenly; Health check every 5 s; 3 consecutive failures mark a backend unhealthy; No retries at the balancer.
steps: Each backend gets 1,000 ÷ 10 = 100 requests per second.
Detection takes up to 3 checks × 5 s = 15 s.
With a 2 s interval and 2 failures to trip: 2 × 2 = 4 s, so about 100 × 4 = 400 failures; with passive health checks (eject after a few real errors) it can be under a second.
cards.note: Aggressive health checks plus passive outlier detection and safe retries cut the damage from about 1,500 failed requests to a few hundred or fewer.

cards.title: Trap: the wrong layer for the job
cards.body: Choosing L4 when you need path-based routing, or L7 for non-HTTP protocols.

cards.title: Health checks
cards.body: The balancer probes each backend, for example GET /healthz every 5 s. After a few failures it stops routing there; after a few passes it adds it back. Active checks catch dead servers before users do; passive checks watch real responses for errors.

questions.prompt: Route /images to one pool and /api to another. Which balancer?

choices.label: An L4 balancer, because it is faster
A forward proxy
An L7 (HTTP) load balancer
DNS round robin

questions.explanation: Only L7 reads the path.

questions.prompt: Which one needs an L4 balancer rather than L7?

choices.label: Canary routing on a request header
Redirecting HTTP to HTTPS
A custom TCP protocol for multiplayer game servers
Routing /api and /static to different pools

questions.explanation: L7 balancers understand HTTP; a custom protocol needs plain TCP forwarding.

questions.prompt: A backend fails three health checks in a row. What does the balancer do?

choices.label: Removes its address from DNS for every client
Restarts the backend’s process and waits for it
Keeps sending it half of its usual traffic
Stops sending it new requests until it passes checks again

questions.explanation: Balancers route around failures; restarting is the orchestrator’s job.

questions.prompt: Order an L7 routing decision.

items.label: Rule matched on path or header

questions.explanation: L7 must parse HTTP before it can match a rule.

questions.prompt: Pick a balancer for HTTPS web traffic that needs path routing.
constraints: TLS should end at the edge

rationaleOptions.label: L7 can read the path once it terminates TLS
L4 only sees IPs and ports, so it cannot route by path
L4 is needed to terminate TLS

rationaleConflicts.r3: TLS termination here is L7 work; an L4 balancer passes the encrypted bytes through.

questions.explanation: Path routing requires reading HTTP, which means L7.

flashcards.back: IP addresses and ports.
HTTP paths, headers, cookies.

title: Forward vs Reverse Proxy
objectives: A reverse proxy fronts servers (TLS, caching, compression); a forward proxy fronts clients.

cards.title: Client-side vs server-side proxies
cards.body: Nginx/Envoy as a reverse proxy hides backends, terminates TLS, compresses and caches. A forward proxy (corporate) sits in front of clients to filter or anonymise outbound traffic.

cards.title: A request through a reverse proxy
cards.body: The proxy terminates TLS, serves cached or compressed responses itself and forwards only the rest to the upstream app.

cards.title: Worked example: what a caching reverse proxy saves the origin
cards.body: Assume: 20,000 requests per second for product pages at peak; 80% of them are cacheable for 60 s at the proxy; Each origin render costs about 20 ms of CPU.
steps: Requests served from the proxy cache = 20,000 × 0.8 = 16,000 per second.
Requests reaching the origin = 20,000 − 16,000 = 4,000 per second.
Origin CPU needed = 4,000 × 0.02 s = 80 CPU-seconds per second, about 80 cores, versus 20,000 × 0.02 = 400 cores without the cache.
That is a 5× reduction in origin capacity.
cards.note: An 80% cache hit rate at the reverse proxy cuts origin load by 5× (from about 400 cores to about 80).

cards.title: Trap: mixing up forward and reverse
cards.body: Mixing up the two. Reverse = server side; forward = client side.

questions.prompt: A company filters which websites employees can visit. What sits in the path?

choices.label: A reverse proxy
A CDN
A forward proxy
An L4 load balancer

questions.explanation: Forward proxies act for clients on outbound traffic.

questions.prompt: Which is a typical reverse-proxy job?

choices.label: Terminate TLS and compress responses for the app servers
Cache public websites for a school network
Hide employees’ IP addresses from websites
Filter which websites employees may visit

questions.explanation: The other three act on the client side, which is forward-proxy work.

questions.prompt: A reverse proxy sits in front of what?

choices.label: The DNS resolver
Your users’ devices, facing outgoing traffic
The database query planner
Your servers, facing incoming client traffic

questions.explanation: Reverse proxies represent servers; forward proxies represent clients.

questions.prompt: Order a request through a reverse proxy.
questions.explanation: The proxy handles cross-cutting work before the app sees the request.

questions.prompt: Static CSS and images are 70% of requests, the proxy does no caching, and app servers sit at 90% CPU. Click the bottleneck.
questions.explanation: Let the reverse proxy cache or serve static files so the app only handles dynamic requests.

flashcards.front: Reverse proxy sits in front of?
flashcards.back: Servers.

flashcards.front: Forward proxy sits in front of?
flashcards.back: Clients.

title: Stateless Services & Sessions
objectives: Explain what makes a service stateless
Decide where session state should live
Weigh sticky sessions against a shared session store

cards.title: What stateless means
cards.body: A stateless service keeps nothing about a user in its own memory between requests. Any instance can serve any request, so the balancer spreads load freely and an instance can die without logging anyone out.

cards.title: Where session state goes
cards.body: Move it out: a shared store such as Redis keyed by session id, or a signed token the client sends each time. The database stays the source of truth for durable data.

cards.title: Sticky sessions
cards.body: Sticky sessions pin a user to one instance with a cookie. It is a quick fix for a stateful app, but load spreads unevenly and the session dies with the instance.

cards.title: A request with external sessions
cards.body: Because the session lives in Redis, the balancer can send each request to any healthy instance and the cart is still there.
steps: Client sends a cookie with the session id
Instance loads the session from Redis
Changes are written back to Redis

cards.title: Trap: carts in server memory
cards.body: Keeping a shopping cart in server memory and then scaling out. Users bounce between instances and their carts vanish. Move the cart to a shared store first.

questions.prompt: After adding a second app server, users randomly lose their carts. Most likely cause?

choices.label: The database cannot handle connections from two servers
Carts live in each server’s memory and requests bounce between servers
Round robin is sending all the traffic to one server
The load balancer strips cookies from every response

questions.explanation: In-memory state breaks as soon as requests can land on different instances.

questions.prompt: What is the main downside of sticky sessions?

choices.label: They add a full round trip to every request
They stop the balancer from health checking
Uneven load, and a session is lost when its instance dies
They require a JWT on every request

questions.explanation: Pinning users ties their state to one machine.

questions.prompt: Where should session state live for a horizontally scaled web app?

choices.label: In each instance’s memory, with sticky sessions turned off
In the load balancer’s memory
In files on each server’s local disk
In a shared store such as Redis, or in a signed token the client sends

questions.explanation: Shared or client-held state lets any instance serve any request.

questions.prompt: Order a request that uses an external session store.

items.label: Instance loads the session from Redis

questions.explanation: The instance holds nothing between requests.

questions.prompt: Choose a session approach for a 20-instance checkout service where sessions must survive deploys.

approaches.label: Sticky sessions
approaches.description: Pin each user to one instance

rationaleOptions.label: Sticky sessions spread load evenly
Sessions survive an instance restart during a deploy
Any instance can serve any request

rationaleConflicts.r3: Pinning users makes load uneven as busy sessions pile up on some instances.

questions.explanation: An external store keeps instances disposable.

flashcards.front: After adding a second app server, users randomly lose their carts. Most likely cause?
flashcards.back: Carts live in each server’s memory and requests bounce between servers. In-memory state breaks as soon as requests can land on different instances.

flashcards.front: What is the main downside of sticky sessions?
flashcards.back: Uneven load, and a session is lost when its instance dies. Pinning users ties their state to one machine.

flashcards.front: Where should session state live for a horizontally scaled web app?
flashcards.back: In a shared store such as Redis, or in a signed token the client sends. Shared or client-held state lets any instance serve any request.

title: Where to Cache
objectives: Caches keep hot data in fast storage to cut latency and offload databases.

cards.title: Why caching works: skewed reads
cards.body: Reads often follow a power law: a small set of keys gets most traffic. Serving them from memory (Redis, local LRU) drops latency from ms to µs and shields the DB.

cards.title: A cache-aside read
cards.body: Check the cache; on a hit return it, on a miss read the database and populate the cache so the next read hits.
steps: Populate the cache with a TTL

cards.title: Worked example: why the last few percent of hit rate matter
cards.body: Assume: Cache hit costs 1 ms, database read costs 10 ms; 100,000 reads per second.
steps: Average latency = hit rate × 1 ms + miss rate × 10 ms.
At 90% hits: 0.9 of reads cost 1 ms and 0.1 cost 10 ms, so 0.9 + 1.0 ≈ 1.9 ms on average; database reads = 100,000 × 0.1 = 10,000 per second.
At 99% hits: 0.99 + 0.1 ≈ 1.09 ms on average; database reads = 100,000 × 0.01 = 1,000 per second.
Going from 90% to 99% cuts database load 10×, even though the hit rate only rose 9 points.
cards.note: Database load is driven by the miss rate: 10% misses means 10,000 DB reads/s, 1% means 1,000. Quote miss rate, not just hit rate, when sizing the database.

cards.title: Trap: caching everything
cards.body: Caching everything blindly. Cache data that is read-heavy and tolerant of brief staleness.

cards.title: Cache layers
cards.body: From the user inward: browser cache, CDN edge, reverse proxy, an in-process cache in each app instance, a shared cache such as Redis, then the database’s own buffer pool. The closer to the user, the faster the hit and the harder it is to invalidate.

questions.prompt: What does a 95% cache hit rate mean?

choices.label: 95% of writes go only to the cache, skipping the database
The cache holds 95% of all the rows in the database
Reads are 95% faster than they were without a cache
95 of every 100 reads are served from cache; 5 go to the database

questions.explanation: Hit rate is about reads served, not data stored.

questions.prompt: 20,000 reads/s with a 90% hit rate. How many reads/s reach the database?
questions.explanation: Design implication: hit rate matters more than it looks. At 95% the database would see 1,000 reads/s, half as many, so a few percent of hit rate can decide whether you need read replicas.

questions.prompt: Which data is the best cache candidate?

choices.label: Click logs written constantly and read once by a batch job
Product pages read thousands of times per update
A wallet balance during a transfer
One-time OTP verification results

questions.explanation: Cache read-heavy data that tolerates brief staleness.

questions.prompt: Fifty app instances each keep an in-process cache instead of sharing Redis. Main downside?

choices.label: Each instance then needs its own database
Each instance has its own copy, so a change must be invalidated in all 50
In-process caches cannot store strings
In-process memory is slower than a network call to Redis

questions.explanation: Local caches are the fastest hit but the hardest to keep consistent.

questions.prompt: Order a cache-aside read.

items.label: Store the result in the cache

questions.explanation: On a hit the flow stops at the cache.

flashcards.back: hits ÷ (hits + misses).
Read-heavy, hot, staleness-tolerant data.

title: Cache Strategies
objectives: Cache-aside loads on miss; write-through writes both; write-behind writes cache then DB asynchronously.

cards.title: Cache-aside, write-through, write-behind
cards.body: Cache-aside: app reads cache, on miss reads DB and sets cache. Write-through: write cache and DB synchronously (fresh, slower writes). Write-behind: write cache, flush DB later (fast, risk of loss).

cards.title: The cache-aside read path
cards.body: On a miss the app reads the database, writes the value to the cache with a TTL and returns it; writes go to the database and invalidate the key.

cards.title: Worked example: what write-behind buys and risks for a like counter
cards.body: Assume: 20,000 likes per second at peak; Flush to the database every 5 seconds, batched per post; On average a hot post receives many likes per window, so each batch row covers many likes.
steps: Direct writes: 20,000 database updates per second.
With write-behind, each flush writes one row per post touched; if 2,000 distinct posts are liked per 5-second window, that is 2,000 updates per flush ÷ 5 s = 400 updates per second.
Risk: if the cache node dies just before a flush, up to 5 s × 20,000 = 100,000 likes are lost.
cards.note: Write-behind turns about 20,000 writes/s into about 400, at the risk of losing up to about 100,000 likes in a crash. Fine for likes, never for payments.

cards.title: Trap: write-behind for money
cards.body: Using write-behind for payments. Losing buffered writes on a crash is unacceptable for money.

questions.prompt: Which strategy can lose writes if the cache node crashes?

choices.label: Write-behind (write-back)
Write-through
Cache-aside with a short TTL
Cache-aside

questions.explanation: Write-behind acknowledges before the database has the data.

questions.prompt: What does write-through give you, and at what cost?

choices.label: Writes go only to the cache and skip the database entirely
Fast writes, but buffered data can be lost if the cache crashes
Cache and database are updated together, so reads are fresh; writes are slower
No cache misses ever, and it costs nothing extra on writes

questions.explanation: Both stores are written synchronously.

questions.prompt: Order a cache-aside read on a miss.

items.label: Set the cache with a TTL

questions.explanation: The application, not the cache, loads data on a miss.

questions.prompt: Pick a caching strategy for a product catalogue.
constraints: A few seconds of staleness is fine

approaches.label: Cache-aside with a TTL
approaches.description: Load on miss, expire after a while

rationaleOptions.label: A TTL bounds staleness after an update
Write-behind is needed to keep reads fresh
Only items people actually view end up cached

rationaleConflicts.r3: Write-behind speeds up writes and risks losing them; it does nothing for read freshness.

questions.explanation: Read-heavy and staleness-tolerant is the classic cache-aside case.

questions.prompt: Why not use write-behind for a payment ledger?

choices.label: It forces every read to go to the database, so the cache is useless
Payment data is not allowed to be stored in Redis under any rules
Buffered writes can be lost in a crash, and losing money records is unacceptable
Write-behind makes reads slower because every read waits for a flush

questions.explanation: Durability matters more than write speed for money.

flashcards.back: Cache-aside (lazy loading).
Losing unflushed writes.

title: Eviction Policies
objectives: When memory is full: LRU, LFU, FIFO or TTL decide what to drop.

cards.title: LRU, LFU and TTL
cards.body: LRU evicts least recently used — good default. LFU keeps frequently used items — good for stable hot sets. TTL expires data by age regardless of use.

cards.title: What happens when the cache is full
cards.body: A new key arrives, the policy picks a victim (least recent, least frequent or expired), the victim is evicted and the new key inserted.

cards.title: Worked example: how big must the cache be for a 90% hit rate?
cards.body: Assume: 10 million products, about 2 KB of cached data each; Popularity is heavily skewed: about 20% of products receive about 90% of views (an illustrative skew; measure yours).
steps: Memory for the hot set = 2,000,000 × 2 KB ≈ 4 GB.
Caching everything would need 10,000,000 × 2 KB ≈ 20 GB.
With LRU or LFU and about 4–5 GB, the cache holds the hot set and reaches roughly 90% hits; the last 10% of hits would cost the other 16 GB.
cards.note: About 4 GB buys roughly 90% hits under this skew; going further costs memory much faster than it adds hits. Size the cache for the hot set, then let the eviction policy keep it hot.

cards.title: Trap: no TTLs at all
cards.body: Never setting TTLs, so stale entries live forever after the source changes.

questions.prompt: Which policy evicts the item not accessed for the longest time?

choices.label: TTL
LFU
FIFO
LRU

questions.explanation: Least recently used.

questions.prompt: A stable set of popular products gets most traffic, but a nightly job reads every product once. Which policy best keeps the popular set cached?

choices.label: FIFO, because it ignores access patterns
LFU, because one read does not make an item frequent
LRU, because the scanned items were used most recently
No policy: a full cache stops accepting keys

questions.explanation: Under LRU the scan pushes out the hot set; LFU keeps items that are used often.

questions.prompt: A price changed in the database, but the cache served the old price for days. What was missing?

choices.label: An LFU eviction policy on the cache
A second cache replica in another zone
A TTL (or explicit invalidation) on the cached price
More cache memory so keys are not evicted

questions.explanation: Eviction only happens under memory pressure; TTLs bound staleness.

questions.prompt: What does FIFO evict?

choices.label: The largest item, to free the most memory
The item used least often over its lifetime
The item inserted earliest, regardless of how often it is used
The item that has gone longest without a read

questions.explanation: FIFO ignores access entirely.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when a full cache gets a new key.
questions.explanation: The policy only decides which key leaves.

flashcards.back: Hash map + doubly linked list.
Stable, skewed hot sets.

title: Stampede/Penetration/Avalanche
objectives: Protect against many simultaneous misses and single overloaded keys.

cards.title: Stampede, penetration, avalanche
cards.body: Stampede: a popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the DB. Fix with request coalescing (single flight), locks, early refresh, and TTL jitter. Hot keys: replicate or add local caches.

cards.title: Surviving a hot key expiring
cards.body: Single-flight lets one request rebuild the value while the others wait for it, so the database sees one read instead of thousands.

cards.title: Worked example: a stampede on one hot key
cards.body: Assume: A trending-deals key is read 50,000 times per second; Rebuilding it takes 200 ms of database queries; The key expires with no protection.
steps: Requests arriving during the 200 ms rebuild window = 50,000 × 0.2 = 10,000.
Without coalescing, up to 10,000 identical rebuild queries hit the database at once.
With single-flight, 1 request rebuilds and the other 9,999 wait or get the stale value.
Database queries per expiry fall from about 10,000 to 1.
cards.note: One unprotected hot key can send about 10,000 identical queries to the database in 200 ms; coalescing makes it one.

cards.title: Trap: identical TTLs
cards.body: Setting identical TTLs on a million keys, so they all expire together.

cards.title: Penetration and avalanche
cards.body: Penetration: requests for keys that do not exist (often bots) miss the cache every time and hit the database; cache the “not found” briefly or check a Bloom filter. Avalanche: many keys expire together, or a cache node dies, and the database takes the full load; add TTL jitter and replicate the cache.

questions.prompt: Thousands of requests miss the same just-expired key at once. Best fix?

choices.label: Lower the TTL so the key refreshes more often than before
Let one request rebuild the key while the others wait (single flight)
Add more database replicas and leave the cache unchanged
Stop caching that key so requests always read the database

questions.explanation: Coalescing turns thousands of identical misses into one database read.

questions.prompt: Bots request random product ids that do not exist; every request misses and hits the database. Fix?

choices.label: Switch eviction from LRU to LFU so hot keys stay in memory
Raise the TTL of existing keys so fewer requests miss the cache
Add TTL jitter so the missing keys expire at different times
Cache the “not found” result briefly, or check a Bloom filter first

questions.explanation: The cache never holds keys that do not exist unless you store the negative answer.

questions.prompt: A million keys were loaded at 9:00 with a one-hour TTL. At 10:00 the database falls over. Fix?

choices.label: Add random jitter to TTLs so expiries spread out
Give the cache more memory
Set every TTL to exactly two hours
Use single flight per key, nothing else

questions.explanation: Identical TTLs make keys expire together; jitter spreads them.

questions.prompt: Order single-flight handling of a hot key.
questions.explanation: Only the lock holder goes to the database.

questions.prompt: The live-score key expires and 50K requests/s miss together. Click where it breaks.
questions.explanation: The database takes every miss at once. Coalescing or early refresh protects it.

flashcards.back: Many concurrent misses for one key overwhelm the DB.
Replicate key, local cache, or split key.

title: CDN
objectives: CDNs cache static and media content close to users, cutting latency and origin load.

cards.title: Edge caching and invalidation
cards.body: Edge PoPs cache assets with TTLs; misses go to origin. Use cache keys, versioned URLs for invalidation, and signed URLs for private media.

cards.title: A user in Pune fetching an asset
cards.body: The nearest PoP serves a cached copy; on a miss it fetches from the origin, stores the object at the edge and serves it.
steps: Store at the edge for its TTL

cards.title: Worked example: egress for a live stream with and without a CDN
cards.body: Assume: 10 million concurrent viewers; Average bitrate 2 Mbit/s (a mix of mobile qualities); Video split into 6-second segments; each edge fetches each segment from the shield once; 500 edge locations.
steps: Total delivery bandwidth = 10,000,000 × 2 Mbit/s = 20,000,000 Mbit/s = 20 Tbit/s, all served by CDN edges.
Without a CDN, the origin itself would have to push about 20 Tbit/s.
With a CDN, each edge fetches each segment about once per rendition, so the origin or shield serves roughly 500 edges × a handful of renditions per segment.
Origin egress ≈ 500 × 2 Mbit/s × 5 renditions = 5,000 Mbit/s = 5 Gbit/s, about 4,000× less than 20 Tbit/s.
cards.note: The CDN carries about 20 Tbit/s at the edges while the origin sends a few Gbit/s. Live streaming at this scale is only possible because each edge fetches each segment once.

cards.title: Trap: purging everything on deploy
cards.body: Purging the whole CDN on every deploy. Use content-hashed filenames so new versions get new URLs.

questions.prompt: Best way to “invalidate” a JavaScript bundle after a deploy?

choices.label: Set the CDN TTL to 0 for every asset so it is never cached at the edge
Purge the whole CDN on every deploy and let the edges refill from origin
Keep the same filename and ask users to hard-refresh after each release
Ship it under a content-hashed filename (app.3f9c.js) and reference the new URL

questions.explanation: New content gets a new URL, so caches never serve the wrong version.

questions.prompt: An IPL final has 20M concurrent viewers at 2 Mbps each. Total egress in Tbps?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: 40 Tbps is far more than any single origin or data centre uplink, so live video at this scale is only deliverable from many CDN edges, often across several CDNs.

questions.prompt: Paid course videos must play only for enrolled students but still come from the CDN. How?

choices.label: Signed URLs that expire
Long TTLs so they stay cached

Serve them from the origin only

questions.explanation: The edge checks the signature and expiry before serving.

title: Redis Deep Dive
objectives: Shared in-memory caches scale out across nodes using sharding and replication.

cards.title: Redis data structures and scaling
cards.body: Redis offers data structures (sorted sets, hashes), persistence, replication and cluster sharding. Memcached is simple, multithreaded key-value. Clients shard keys with consistent hashing.

cards.title: A write in Redis Cluster
cards.body: The client hashes the key to a slot, sends the write to that slot's primary, and the primary replicates to its replica asynchronously.

cards.title: Worked example: a live leaderboard for a quiz show
cards.body: Assume: 5 million players in one sorted set; About 100 bytes per entry including member ID and skiplist plus hash overhead (an estimate; check with MEMORY USAGE); 200,000 score updates per second at peak.
steps: Memory = 5,000,000 × 100 bytes = 500,000,000 bytes ≈ 500 MB, which fits easily on one node.
ZADD and ZRANK are O(log N); log2 of 5 million is about 22, so each operation is a few dozen steps.
200,000 updates per second is above what one node handles comfortably, so split players into shards (for example 4 sorted sets by player ID), giving 50,000 updates per second per shard.
Global top 10 = take the top 10 from each of the 4 shards (40 entries) and merge them.
cards.note: About 500 MB of memory and O(log N) updates: sorted sets make a 5-million-player leaderboard cheap. Shard by player and merge the per-shard top 10s for the global top 10.

cards.title: Trap: one node, no replica
cards.body: Using a single Redis node for critical data with no replica — one restart wipes the hot set and floods the DB.

questions.prompt: Which Redis structure fits a game leaderboard?

choices.label: A hash of user → score, sorted in the app
A list, sorted on every read
One string key per user
A sorted set (ZADD, ZREVRANGE)

questions.explanation: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score.

questions.prompt: When is Memcached enough instead of Redis?

choices.label: Plain key-value caching with no need for data structures or persistence
When you need a sorted leaderboard updated in place
When the cached data must survive a restart of the node
When you need built-in replication across several nodes

questions.explanation: Memcached is simple and multithreaded, without Redis’s extras.

questions.prompt: A single Redis node with no replica restarts at peak. What happens?

choices.label: Clients fail over to a replica transparently
Only writes fail; reads keep working
The hot set is gone and the database is flooded with misses
Redis reloads everything from memory instantly

questions.explanation: Critical caches need replicas.

questions.prompt: Order a write through a sharded Redis setup.
questions.explanation: Replication is asynchronous, after the primary applies the write.

Memcached’s multithreading gives it sorted sets
